p.x:
Last year I felt tired all the time. I went to bed late, often after midnight, and I watched videos on my phone in bed. In the morning, I couldn't hear my alarm, and I was always late for work. I ate a lot of sugar and salty snacks, and I was a little overweight.
So I decided to change. Now I go to bed at 10:30 and leave my phone in the kitchen. I wake up at 6:00 and stretch for five minutes. Three times a week I jog in the park before work, and on Sundays I do yoga with my sister.
I also eat more fruit, and I take a vitamin every morning. Sometimes I have a short nap after lunch at the weekend. My wife says I don't snore any more, and I don't yawn at my desk. I even have good dreams now! It's the best change I have ever made.

Many people believe that being healthy requires a complete change of lifestyle. In fact, doctors say that small habits, repeated every day, can make a big difference.
First, don't skip breakfast. A balanced breakfast with protein, such as eggs, and fibre, such as whole-grain bread, gives you energy until lunch. Second, think about caffeine. One or two cups of coffee in the morning are fine, but coffee after 3 p.m. can stop you from sleeping well.
Third, check your posture. Many office workers sit badly for hours, which causes back and neck pain. Stand up and walk around every hour. Fourth, learn to manage stress. Some people find that a short walk or a few deep breaths helps them feel calmer.
Finally, count your sleep, not just your calories. If you wake up feeling refreshed, you are probably sleeping enough. If you feel drowsy during the day, you may need to go to bed earlier.

p.t: Why Sleep Is Not a Luxury
p.x:
In many modern societies, sleeping less is seen as a sign of hard work. Business leaders proudly claim to need only four or five hours a night. Yet scientists increasingly warn that sleep deprivation is a serious public-health problem.
Sleep is regulated by our circadian rhythm, an internal clock that responds to light and darkness. When we stay up late under bright screens, this rhythm is disturbed, and the body struggles to produce the hormones that make us sleepy. The result is not only fatigue the next day but, over time, a higher risk of heart disease, weight gain and depression. Lack of sleep also appears to slow the metabolism, which explains why tired people often feel sluggish and crave sugary food.
The good news is that sleep habits can be improved. Experts recommend keeping a consistent schedule, even at weekends, and avoiding heavy meals and alcohol before bed. Staying hydrated during the day matters too, although drinking large amounts in the evening may wake you up at night. Some people find that meditation helps calm a busy mind.
Ultimately, researchers argue, we should prioritise sleep in the same way we value a diet rich in nutrients or regular exercise. Like food, sleep is best enjoyed not in moderation, but in sufficient quantity.
